title: Not to abolish (Matthew 5:17–20)
hookLine: he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them

cards: Some people picture Jesus throwing out the old rulebook. Out with the laws, in with love. It's a popular idea, and it's the very thing Jesus heads off next in the sermon.

His listeners were crowds from Galilee, Jerusalem and Judea, people who knew the Torah from the synagogue. Some may have wondered: is this new teacher against it? Before he says anything else, he answers.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." The law here is the Torah, the first five books of the Bible, Genesis to Deuteronomy.
Torah is usually translated law, but the Hebrew word means more like teaching, or instruction: the way God shows people how to live. For Jews it's the heart of scripture, and it still is.
Then: till heaven and earth pass, "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." A jot is the yod, a Hebrew letter hardly bigger than an apostrophe.
A tittle is a tiny stroke, the little hook that tells one Hebrew letter from another. Not even that much will be lost.
So what does fulfill mean? Christians read it several ways.
Some say Jesus fulfills the law by living it completely and bringing out its deepest intent, which the rest of the chapter goes on to do.
Some also say parts of it, like the temple sacrifices, find their fulfillment in him.
Churches differ on exactly how the law applies to Christians today, and Jews, for their part, continue to live by the Torah as their covenant with God.
Then: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees.

teach.h: NOT TO DESTROY, BUT TO FULFIL.
teach.b: In his day the Pharisees were known for taking the law seriously, down to the details. He isn't lowering the bar. He's saying: go deeper, all the way to the heart.

how: Christians read the Old Testament in worship alongside the Gospels, and in churches that follow a lectionary, a Sunday service often includes a reading from the law or the prophets.

games.why: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets." not one jot or tittle will pass away.

practice: The words Jesus means are, first of all, the Torah, still read, sung and studied in synagogues week by week.
Think of a Jewish neighbor, friend or coworker, or Jewish families you've never met, gathering around those same scrolls, and hold them in mind with respect and gratitude.
If you pray, you can give thanks for the Torah and for the people who have carried it through the generations.
